title: Node.js Brings Debounce, Throttle, and PKCS#12 Parsing Into Core Modules
gist: Node.js 26.10.0 moved long-requested utilities into core: util.debounce() and util.throttle() in node:util, util.markPromiseAsHandled(), a crypto.parsePKCS12() API for .p12/.pfx bundles, and VFS-backed library loading in node:ffi. The additions continue a trend of shrinking reliance on userland packages such as lodash and node-forge, narrowing the standard-library gap with Bun and Deno and reducing supply-chain exposure; Node.js 26 is now Active LTS ("Lithium") through April 2029.

insights.claim: Node.js 26.10.0 added util.debounce() and util.throttle() to the core node:util module, replacing rate-limiting helpers that were among the most commonly vendored dependencies, typically pulled from lodash or the throttle-debounce package.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Core absorption of popular micro-packages erodes the role of utility libraries like lodash in new Node.js code.
insights.locator: The headline change is the arrival of util.debounce() and util.throttle()

insights.claim: James M Snell landed Node.js's debounce and throttle helpers in a single pull request, and Matteo Collina said he uses these utilities in essentially every app.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Endorsement from prominent maintainers indicates broad demand and fast adoption of the built-ins.
insights.locator: James M Snell landed both in a single pull request

insights.claim: After contributors ljharb and bakkot flagged that an AbortSignal only transitions to aborted once, Node.js reworked the debounce/throttle signal to cancel every future invocation and added a leading-edge option so the first call fires immediately.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: API design review by TC39-adjacent contributors shaped semantics; developers migrating from lodash should check behavioral differences.
insights.locator: Contributors ljharb and bakkot flagged the awkwardness

insights.claim: Node.js also added util.markPromiseAsHandled(), an explicit way for framework authors to tell the runtime a promise has been handled, addressing long-running confusion around unhandled-rejection signalling.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Gives framework vendors a cleaner primitive to avoid spurious unhandled-rejection crashes.

themes.theme: PKCS#12 parsing and VFS in node:ffi

insights.claim: Node.js's new crypto.parsePKCS12() API wraps OpenSSL's d2i_PKCS12_bio() and PKCS12_parse() to return privateKey, certificate and additionalCertificates from .p12/.pfx bundles, removing the need to shell out to the openssl CLI or depend on packages like node-forge.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Reduces dependence on third-party crypto packages, a meaningful security and supply-chain improvement for enterprise Node.js apps handling certificates.
insights.locator: crypto.parsePKCS12() closes a different long-standing gap

insights.claim: Matteo Collina and Philipp Dunkel extended Node.js's experimental Virtual File System so node:ffi can load libraries straight from a mounted VFS using the anonymous memfd technique native addons use on Linux, and the patch fixed a dlopen bug that silently broke addon loading from the real filesystem.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: VFS plus FFI loading moves Node.js toward self-contained single-binary distribution of apps with native code.
insights.locator: The experimental Virtual File System has also grown further

insights.claim: Node.js's run of standard-library additions continues a visible trend of reducing reliance on userland utilities, narrowing the gap with Bun and Deno, which have tended to ship richer standard libraries by default.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Node.js is defending its runtime share against Bun and Deno by matching their batteries-included approach.

insights.claim: Moving debounce, throttle and PKCS#12 parsing into Node.js core cuts a handful of small dependencies out of typical node_modules trees, with supply-chain security implications.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Fewer transitive micro-dependencies shrink npm supply-chain attack surface, relevant to software-security vendors and enterprise risk.
insights.quote: cutting a handful of small dependencies out of typical node_modules trees
insights.locator: The shift also has supply-chain implications

insights.claim: Node.js 26 has moved to Active LTS under the codename "Lithium" with support through April 2029, and v26.11.0 followed 26.10.0 with further Buffer and http helpers.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Enterprises can standardize on Node.js 26 with a support horizon to April 2029.
insights.locator: The changes landed first on the Current line
